title: At the food stall
goal: Order food and drinks at a mamak restaurant, a hawker stall or a food court — the first place that really tests your Malay, and the place where mistakes are forgiven fastest.
bekal: order food and drinks the way real people do
use *nak*, *boleh*, *tolong* and *sila* in the right places
read a mamak menu without guessing

dialogs.title: Dialogue — A mamak stall at night
dialogs.intro: Ten o'clock at night. Haziq takes Sarah to the mamak restaurant across from the college — open twenty-four hours and full of people at all sorts of odd times.

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.id: What would you like to eat, young lady?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Roti canai dua, teh tarik satu. Sarah, awak nak apa?
lines.id: Two roti canai, one teh tarik. Sarah, what do you want?
lines.literal: roti canai two, tea pulled one. Sarah, you want what?

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.text: Ada. Nak pedas ke tak pedas?
lines.literal: there-is. want spicy or not spicy?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Pedas sikit je. Dengan air apa yang tak manis?
lines.id: Just a little spicy. And what drink isn't sweet?
lines.literal: spicy little only. with drink what that not sweet?

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.text: Teh o kosong. Tak ada gula langsung.
lines.id: Black tea, plain. No sugar at all.
lines.literal: tea o empty. not there-is sugar at-all.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Okey, teh o kosong satu. Sejuk boleh?
lines.id: OK, one plain black tea. Can I have it cold?
lines.literal: okay, tea o empty one. cold can?

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.text: Boleh. Teh o ais kosong. Makan sini ke bungkus?
lines.id: Sure. Iced black tea, no sugar. Eating here or takeaway?
lines.literal: can. tea o ice empty. eat here or wrap?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Haziq, sedap tak nasi lemak sini?
lines.id: Haziq, is the nasi lemak here good?
lines.literal: Haziq, tasty not nasi lemak here?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.id: Crazy good. The sambal really packs a punch.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nanti kita kira sekali ya. Saya belanja.
lines.id: Let's pay all together later. My treat.
lines.literal: later we count once yes. I treat.

notes: **Nak** (from *hendak*) is the most frequent word in Malaysian conversation. It means **want**, and also marks the near future ("going to"). *Nak makan apa?* = what do you want to eat? *Saya nak balik* = I'm going home. The formal forms are *hendak* or *mahu*, but you'll rarely hear them in speech.
**Air** means **drink** in general, not just water. *Nak air apa?* = "What would you like to drink?" For plain water people say *air kosong* ("empty water") or *air suam* (warm water).

**Kosong** at a stall means **no sugar**. So *teh o kosong* = tea, no milk, no sugar. Mamak drink orders work like a code: *teh* (with milk), *teh o* (no milk), *ais* (iced), *kosong* (no sugar), *kurang manis* (less sweet), *peng* (iced, from Hokkien).
**Bungkus** = to wrap, i.e. takeaway. The slang word is **tapau** (from Cantonese), and it's what you'll hear most: *nak tapau* = I want it to go.
**Sekejap** = a moment, for a bit. It's everywhere in Malaysian speech. The short form is *kejap*: *kejap ya* = just a sec.

grammars.title: Four ways to ask — and when to use which
body: English uses "please" for almost everything. Malay splits requests across four words, and choosing wrong sounds off — not a grammar mistake, but the wrong tone.
after: ⚠️ The most common learner mistake: using **sila** to ask for something. *Sila* is the "please" of "please, have a seat" — you're offering, not asking. *Sila duduk* = "please sit down" (you're the host). To ask for help, use *tolong*: *Tolong bungkuskan* = please wrap it up for me.

The safest order pattern in any stall: **[item] + [number]**, with no verb at all. *Teh tarik satu.* *Roti canai dua.* *Nasi lemak tiga bungkus.* This is exactly what Malaysians themselves say, and it's quicker than a full sentence.

blocks.text: A *kedai mamak* is an Indian-Muslim eatery that stays open most of the night and is where everyone in Malaysia hangs out. Menus are rarely translated, so here's what you need to know:

head: Dish
What it is
Closest English idea
rows: coconut rice, sambal, anchovies, egg, cucumber
flaky layered flatbread, eaten with dal curry
rice with a choice of curries, pick your own
noodles in thick gravy / in soto broth
water spinach stir-fried with shrimp paste

blocks.text: Note **telur mata kerbau** — a fried egg is "buffalo's-eye egg" in Malay (Indonesian says "cow's-eye"; English says "sunny side up"). And **belacan** is fermented shrimp paste, the backbone of many sambals.

head: Order
What you get
rows: milk tea "pulled" until frothy — the national drink
no sugar — added at the end of the order
iced Milo / iced Milo heaped with Milo powder
rose syrup with milk, bright pink

blocks.text: The order of an order: **drink + temperature + sugar**. *Teh o ais kosong* = tea, no milk, iced, no sugar. *Kopi kurang manis* = coffee with milk, less sugar. Once you get the sequence, you can build any order without memorizing the list.

blocks.title: Stall phrases you need
items: **Ada … tak?** — Do you have …? (*Ada nasi lemak tak?*)
**Jangan letak …** — Don't put in … (*Jangan letak cili.* = no chilli)
**Kurang pedas / kurang manis** — Less spicy / less sweet.
**Makan sini ke bungkus?** — Eating here or takeaway? (you'll be asked this)
**Berapa semua?** — How much is it altogether?
**Halal ke?** — Is it halal? (an ordinary question, not awkward at all in Malaysia)

head: Malay
English
Note
rows: *Haus* is also used, but *dahaga* is more common.

blocks.text: Intensifiers in Malaysian speech: **sangat** (very, standard), **sungguh** (rather formal), **betul** (*sedap betul* = really tasty), **gila** (crazy, very casual), **giler** (its slang spelling) — and most typical of all, **sangat** placed **after** the adjective: *sedap sangat*, *pedas sangat*, *mahal sangat*. In formal Malay *sangat* goes before; in conversation it almost always comes after. This one small change makes you sound instantly Malaysian.
